title: Review: plans and the future
why: The unit review brings together the future, the near future and intentions, smikhut, and pi'el around a real-life situation: organizing an outing with friends. It wraps up the "Plans and the Future" unit before the "Living in Israel" unit.

Reminder: the future

In the future, a prefix attaches to the front of the root: אֶ (I), תִּ (you, she, you plural), יִ (he, they), נִ (we). Three forms add an ending: ־ִי (you, f.) and ־וּ (you plural, they).

For a plan that's coming soon or already decided, the near future is more common in speech: אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ לִקְנוֹת (a man) / אֲנִי הוֹלֶכֶת לִקְנוֹת (a woman), \"I'm going to buy.\"

Remember: תִּכְתֹּב = you will write (m.) or she will write.

Plans and compound nouns

To talk about your plans: מִתְכַּוֵּן / מִתְכַּוֶּנֶת לְ־ (to intend to), מְתַכְנֵן / מְתַכְנֶנֶת (to plan), הָיִיתִי רוֹצֶה / רוֹצָה (I would like).

אֲנַחְנוּ מִתְכַּוְּנִים לְטַיֵּל בַּשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא.We intend to take a trip next week. [anakhnu mitkavnim letayel ba-shavu'a ha-ba]

Smikhut joins two nouns: the first one sometimes changes (בַּיִת → בֵּית, ־ָה → ־ַת), the article goes on the second, and an adjective at the end agrees with the first.

נִפְגֹּשׁ חֲבֵרִים בְּבֵית הַקָּפֶה הֶחָדָשׁ.We'll meet up with friends at the new café. [nifgosh khaverim be-veit ha-kafe he-khadash]

To organize an outing, you now have everything you need:

For \"let's meet at…,\" Israelis say נִפָּגֵשׁ (nipagesh, another binyan, to learn as a set phrase): נִפָּגֵשׁ בְּתַחֲנַת הָרַכֶּבֶת. נִפְגֹּשׁ, on the other hand, needs an object: נִפְגֹּשׁ חֲבֵרִים (we'll meet up with friends).
